questions.q: Per this lesson, how do Chainlink Price Feeds implement the "real fix" described in Lesson 17?
options: Prices are set manually by a committee once per day
Your contract makes a direct HTTP call to a price API at read time
A single Chainlink-operated server fetches the price and pushes it on-chain
Independent node operators each fetch a price from multiple sources, and those answers are aggregated into one published value your contract reads
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties Price Feeds to Lesson 17's independent-nodes-plus-aggregation pattern — your contract only reads the already-aggregated result.

questions.q: In the real consumer contract shown in this lesson, what does `latestRoundData()` return, and how much of it does the example actually use?
options: A string-formatted price with a currency symbol already attached
A boolean indicating whether the price is still valid
Five values (roundId, answer, startedAt, updatedAt, answeredInRound); the example destructures away everything except `answer`
Only a single int256 answer value, with no other data
questions.explain: The guide shows the exact destructuring `(, int256 answer,,,) = dataFeed.latestRoundData();`, keeping only the answer out of five returned values.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the feed's contract address used in the consumer contract's constructor?
options: It's hardcoded, because every supported asset pair on every supported network has its own fixed address published by Chainlink
It's the same address across every network and every asset pair
It changes every time the price updates, so it must be fetched via an API call first
It's generated dynamically at deploy time by the Chainlink CLI
questions.explain: The lesson explains that each asset pair, per network, has its own fixed, published feed address hardcoded into the constructor.

questions.q: In the Remix walkthrough shown in this lesson, what does selecting "Injected Provider" actually do?
options: It injects a mock price feed so no real testnet funds are needed
It automatically selects the correct Solidity compiler version
It publishes the subgraph to Subgraph Studio
It hands off transaction signing to a real connected wallet extension like MetaMask, instead of using Remix's own built-in test accounts
questions.explain: The lesson and its screenshot specifically show Injected Provider as the option that routes signing through a real wallet, unlike Remix's own test environments.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a raw integer returned from a price feed need before it's a human-readable price?
options: It must be multiplied by the current block number
Nothing — the raw integer returned is already in dollars and cents
It needs to be scaled by the feed's `decimals()` value — for example, dividing an 8-decimal feed's raw answer appropriately
It needs to be converted from Celsius to Fahrenheit
questions.explain: The lesson explains the returned integer is scaled by the feed's decimals value (commonly 8 for USD feeds), and must be divided out for a human-readable price.
